topic.title: kitne ka liya
topic.claim: When your mother asks what something cost, you halve the price. It isn't a lie; it's a currency conversion that spares her the worry.
topic.moment: Mummy asks 'kitne ka liya?' about your new shoes and you hear yourself say half.

turn.believed: Lying about prices is hiding your spending.
turn.actually: It's sparing her the worry, and she does it to you too.

topic.because: She hears the price in the money of the years she ran the house on one salary, so the real number becomes a worry about you.
topic.payoff: Both of you halve prices so nobody has to worry about the other.
topic.send_to: the sibling who also says 'sale tha'

paragraphs: When mummy asks "kitne ka liya?", you say half the price.
That isn't a lie. It's a currency conversion.
You hear yourself say "₹1,800, sale tha."
You didn't plan it. It just came out.
She hears what ₹4,000 meant in the years she ran the house on one salary, counting every note before the month ended.
So the real number isn't a price to her. It's a worry.
Is the child saving anything? Who taught them to spend like this?
Halving the price is how you take that worry off her.
You're not hiding the shoes. You're hiding what that number does to her.
She knows this trick, because she plays it on you.
Ask what her last saree cost.
Two people in one house, both halving prices,
so nobody has to worry about the other.

ledger.text: Parents who ran a household on a single tight income hear a stated price not as a number but as a measure of worry, shaped by their years of counting every rupee; because of this, telling them a lower price than what was actually paid removes that worry rather than deceiving them, which is why halving the price is read as care, not a lie.
ledger.sentence: Because mummy doesn't hear ₹4,000. She hears what ₹4,000 meant in the years she ran the house on one salary, counting every note before the month ended. So the real number isn't a price to her. It's a worry. Halving the price is how you take that worry off her. You're not hiding the shoes. You're hiding what that number does to her.

mechanism.broken_premise: none — every element of the argument is opinion or interpretation, not a falsifiable claim about how a price, fee, law, contract or market works
mechanism.actual_mechanism: The post makes no testable factual claim about pricing, tax, fees, or how any product or market works. Its load-bearing moves — that a parent 'hears' a price as accumulated worry, that quoting a lower number 'removes worry rather than deceives,' and that this reads as care — are all interpretations of motive and feeling, which are explicitly out of scope to falsify. The only literal fact (saying ₹1,800 for a ₹4,000 purchase states a number lower than what was paid) is acknowledged by the post itself; whether that counts as 'a lie' or 'care' is a reading of intent, not a mechanism.

alt_texts: When mummy asks "kitne ka liya?", you say half the price. That isn't a lie. It's a currency conversion.
The shoes cost ₹4,000. You hear yourself say "₹1,800, sale tha." You didn't plan it. It just came out.
Because mummy doesn't hear ₹4,000. She hears what ₹4,000 meant in the years she ran the house on one salary, counting every note before the month ended.
So the real number isn't a price to her. It's a worry. Is the child saving anything? Who taught them to spend like this?
Halving the price is how you take that worry off her. You're not hiding the shoes. You're hiding what that number does to her.
She knows this trick, because she plays it on you. Ask what her last saree cost. "Arre, sasta tha." It wasn't.
Two people in one house, both halving prices, so nobody has to worry about the other.

history.point: You tell your mum a cheaper price than you actually paid because the real number would worry her, and it turns out she's been doing the exact same thing to you.
history.reason: The real price doesn't register to her as a price, it registers as a memory of struggling to run the house on one salary, so a high number becomes a worry about whether you're spending/saving right, not just information.
ideas: lying about prices to each other is a way of protecting each other from money-worry, not deception
